newsitem.title: USA: BPA price structure shakes up West U.S. power trad.
newsitem.headline: BPA price structure shakes up West U.S. power trad.

text.p: The Bonneville Power Administration's move this week to post separate prices for power and transmission has shaken up spot trade in the region and may create competitive opportunities, market sources said.
"They don't have a transportation advantage anymore," said an Oregon trader. "Now they are taking transmission service under their own tariff."

Although Federal Energy Regulatory Commission rules requiring utilities to split transmission from generation take effect in November, BPA implemented its new tariffs on October 1, the start date for its new five-year rate contracts.
He noted that BPA's marketing side will continue to pay fixed transmission rates, absorbing any discount to customers.
"At the beginning of the week our COB price was way too high--more than $23.00 (per megawatt hour)," the Bonneville trader added. "But the raw energy price was too low."
In addition, BPA's power marketing group can't buy hourly surplus firm transmission but instead must buy in blocks of light load hours, heavy load hours or 24 hours, he said.
As a result, Bonneville early this week was offering only non-firm transmission, but switched for Friday pre-schedulings to selling firm power only in blocks.
Bonneville has also offered different transmission rates for non-firm vs. firm power, leading some market sources to expect greater interest in the lower-cost non-firm power.
But those differentials have moved in different directions over the course of the week, with transmission for non-firm hourly power last priced at a premium to firm block deals.
Sources also noted that higher net prices for Bonneville sales into California and the Southwest may well help boost prices in those regions generally.
"With higher prices down south, utilities in California will fire up (thermal) units faster" than they would otherwise, said a Northwest trader.

Another trade source agreed that natural gas-fired power is cheaper than BPA's rolled-in COB prices, but said there is not a big need for the extra supplies this time of year, when mild autumn temperatures moderate electricity demand.
"People are kind of riding it up and down. There is still no great cause for alarm," he added.
Traders also questioned the viability of long-distance transmissions from the Southwest to the Northwest under the new transmission tariffs.
"You are looking at a $2.50 (per MWh) charge just to get across COB," said one market source.
